lessons.title: SELinux basics: modes, contexts and types
lessons.goal:
Learn what SELinux adds to normal permissions, how to read the label on a file or process, and the three modes.

Why it matters: on Red Hat family systems SELinux is on by default, and "permission denied although the mode is right" is very often an SELinux denial. Switching it off is the wrong reaction; reading the label is the right one.

setup.note: Steps with sudo create a test web directory `/srv/lab` and a copy of `cat` labelled as a web server binary, then remove both. Needs SELinux in enforcing mode (the default on Oracle Linux and Red Hat).
commands: sudo rm -rf /srv/lab /usr/local/bin/lab-cat; sudo semanage fcontext -d '/srv/lab(/.*)?' 2>/dev/null; true

steps.title: What SELinux is
steps.text: SELinux is a **mandatory access control** system. Every process and every file has a **security context** (label). A **policy** written by the distribution lists exactly which process types may do what to which object types. Normal permissions (owner, mode) are checked first; SELinux is a second, independent check that even root cannot bypass.

run.cmd: getenforce
sestatus | grep -E '^(SELinux status|Current mode|Loaded policy name)' | tr -s ' ' ' '
run.output:
SELinux status: enabled
Loaded policy name: targeted
Current mode: enforcing

steps.title: Modes
steps.text: **Enforcing**: the policy is applied and violations are blocked and logged. **Permissive**: violations are only logged (for debugging). **Disabled**: off (needs a reboot to change). `setenforce 0` switches to permissive until reboot; it is a diagnostic tool, not a fix.

run.cmd: cat /sys/fs/selinux/enforce; echo
grep -E '^SELINUX=' /etc/selinux/config

steps.title: A label has four fields
steps.text: `user:role:type:level`. The part that matters for daily work is the **type**: names ending in `_t` for processes (`sshd_t`) and objects (`etc_t`, `httpd_sys_content_t`). Policy rules say "type A may read type B". Your own shell:

run.cmd: id -Z

steps.title: Labels on files
steps.text: `ls -Z` shows the context of files. The binary `/usr/sbin/sshd` has type `sshd_exec_t`: when it is executed from a service, the process type changes to `sshd_t` (a **domain transition**).

run.cmd: ls -Z /usr/sbin/sshd /etc/passwd /etc/shadow /var/log/messages | awk '{print $1, $2}' | sed 's/^[^:]*:[^:]*://' | sed 's/:s0 / /'

steps.title: Labels on processes
steps.text: `ps -Z` (or `ps -eZ`) shows the domain of each process. Daemons run in their own confined domains; your interactive session is `unconfined_t`, which the policy allows almost everything.

run.cmd: ps -eZ | awk '$NF ~ /^(sshd|crond|chronyd|auditd)$/ {print $1, $NF}' | sed -E 's/^[^:]*:[^:]*://; s/:s0.*( [a-z]+)$/\1/' | sort -u
run.output:
auditd_t auditd
chronyd_t chronyd
crond_t crond
sshd_t sshd

steps.under: Labels are stored in the **extended attributes** of files (`security.selinux`), in the kernel's process table for processes, and in the packet/port tables for network objects (`semanage port -l`). The SELinux **access vector cache** answers most checks without asking the policy again.

quiz.q: Which SELinux mode only logs violations?
Which part of the context do you usually have to care about?
Where is a file's SELinux label stored?
Is `setenforce 0` a fix for a denial?
options: No: it is for diagnosis; fix the label, boolean or policy
quiz.explain: Keep enforcing and fix the cause.

check.scenario: A colleague says: "the web server cannot read the new site directory, I will disable SELinux." What do you advise?
check.answer: Do not disable it. Check the denial (`ausearch -m avc -ts recent` / `journalctl -t setroubleshoot`), compare labels (`ls -Z`), and relabel the content with the web content type (`semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t '/srv/site(/.*)?'` then `restorecon -Rv /srv/site`). Use `setenforce 0` only briefly to confirm that SELinux is the cause.

lessons.title: Labels, booleans and reading denials
lessons.goal:
Reproduce the most common SELinux problem (a wrongly labelled file), see the denial in the audit log, fix it permanently, and use a boolean.

Why it matters: this is the routine workflow: read the denial, decide whether it is a label, a boolean or genuinely new behaviour, and fix the smallest thing.

setup.note: Steps with sudo create a test web directory `/srv/lab` and a copy of `cat` labelled as a web server binary, then remove both. Needs SELinux in enforcing mode (the default on Oracle Linux and Red Hat).
commands: sudo rm -rf /srv/lab /usr/local/bin/lab-cat; sudo semanage fcontext -d '/srv/lab(/.*)?' 2>/dev/null; true

steps.title: A confined program and a file
steps.text: We copy `cat` and label the copy `httpd_exec_t`, the type of the web server binary. When systemd starts it, the process runs in the `httpd_t` domain, exactly like a real web server. The web content directory has the default label `var_t`.

run.cmd: sudo mkdir -p /srv/lab && echo 'hello web' | sudo tee /srv/lab/index.html > /dev/null; ls -Z /srv/lab/index.html | awk '{print $1}' | cut -d: -f3
sudo cp /usr/bin/cat /usr/local/bin/lab-cat && sudo chcon -t httpd_exec_t /usr/local/bin/lab-cat; ls -Z /usr/local/bin/lab-cat | awk '{print $1}' | cut -d: -f3

steps.title: The denial
steps.text: Run the "web server" as a service as **root** and ask it to read the file. Root passes the normal permission check, but the policy does not allow `httpd_t` to read `var_t`.

run.cmd: sudo systemd-run --pipe --wait --collect -q /usr/local/bin/lab-cat /srv/lab/index.html; echo "exit code: $?"

steps.after: Root got `Permission denied`. Normal permissions are fine: SELinux said no.

steps.title: Find it in the audit log
steps.text: Denials are logged as **AVC** records. `ausearch -m avc` finds them; `-i` translates numbers to names. The key fields: the **source** context (who), the **target** context (what), the class and the permission.

run.cmd: sleep 1; sudo ausearch --input-logs -m avc -ts recent -c lab-cat -i 2>/dev/null | grep -o 'denied  { [a-z_ ]* } for .*' | sed -E 's/pid=[0-9]+ //; s/ino=[0-9]+ //; s/dev="[^"]*" //; s/ permissive=[01]//; s/system_u:system_r://; s/unconfined_u:object_r://; s/:s0//g' | tail -n 1 | cut -c1-200
run.output: denied  { read } for  comm=lab-cat name=index.html scontext=httpd_t tcontext=var_t tclass=file

steps.title: audit2why explains it
steps.text: `audit2why` translates a denial into a reason: here a missing allow rule, that is, the label is not one the policy lets this domain use.

run.cmd: sudo ausearch --input-logs -m avc -ts recent -c lab-cat 2>/dev/null | audit2why 2>&1 | grep -E 'Was caused by|Missing' | sed 's/^[[:space:]]*//'
run.output:
Was caused by:
Missing type enforcement (TE) allow rule.
Was caused by:
Missing type enforcement (TE) allow rule.

steps.title: Fix 1: relabel (temporary)
steps.text: `chcon` changes a label immediately, but it is **lost** at the next relabel or `restorecon`. It is good for testing.

run.cmd: sudo chcon -R -t httpd_sys_content_t /srv/lab; ls -Z /srv/lab/index.html | awk '{print $1}' | cut -d: -f3
sudo systemd-run --pipe --wait --collect -q /usr/local/bin/lab-cat /srv/lab/index.html; echo "exit code: $?"

steps.title: Fix 2: record the rule (permanent)
steps.text: `semanage fcontext` stores a **file-context rule** in the policy store; `restorecon` applies the rules to the files. This survives relabeling. First we show that `restorecon` undoes a temporary `chcon`, then we add the rule.

run.cmd: sudo restorecon -Rv /srv/lab | sed -E 's/ from .* to .*:([a-z_]+):s0$/ -> \1/' | cut -c1-90
sudo semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t '/srv/lab(/.*)?'; sudo restorecon -Rv /srv/lab | sed -E 's/ from .* to .*:([a-z_]+):s0$/ -> \1/' | cut -c1-90
sudo restorecon -Rv /srv/lab | wc -l | awk '{print $1, "changes needed on the next run"}'
run.output: 0 changes needed on the next run

steps.title: Booleans: switches in the policy
steps.text: Some behaviour is too site-specific to hard-code, so the policy has **booleans**. For example `httpd_can_network_connect` lets web server processes make outgoing network connections (to a database or an API). `setsebool` changes the runtime value (add `-P` to make it permanent).

run.cmd: getsebool httpd_can_network_connect
sudo setsebool httpd_can_network_connect on; getsebool httpd_can_network_connect; sudo setsebool httpd_can_network_connect off; getsebool httpd_can_network_connect
sudo semanage boolean -l | grep -E '^httpd_can_network_connect ' | tr -s ' ' ' ' | cut -c1-90
run.output: httpd_can_network_connect (off , off) Allow httpd to can network connect

steps.title: Clean up
steps.text: Remove the rule, the test directory and the program.

run.cmd: sudo semanage fcontext -d '/srv/lab(/.*)?'; sudo rm -rf /srv/lab /usr/local/bin/lab-cat; echo cleaned

steps.under: The order of fixing: (1) a **boolean** if one exists for the behaviour, (2) a **file context** if the label is wrong, (3) a **port label** (`semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 8888`) for a non-standard port, and only last (4) a **local policy module** (`audit2allow -M mypolicy`), reviewed carefully, because it widens what the domain may do.

quiz.q: A confined service gets Permission denied on a file; the mode is right. Where do you look next?
options: The AVC denial in the audit log (ausearch -m avc)
quiz.explain: SELinux logs the exact source, target and permission.

quiz.q: What is the difference between `chcon` and `semanage fcontext`+`restorecon`?
options: chcon is temporary; the semanage rule survives relabeling

quiz.q: Which is the preferred fix order?
options: Boolean, file context, port label, then local policy

check.scenario: After moving a website to /data/www, Apache returns 403 although `chmod -R a+rX` was applied. Give the exact commands to fix it properly.
check.answer: `sudo semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t '/data/www(/.*)?'` and `sudo restorecon -Rv /data/www`. For uploads the web server must write to, use `httpd_sys_rw_content_t`. Verify with `ls -Zd /data/www` and watch `ausearch -m avc -ts recent`. If Apache also needs to connect out (PHP calling an API), set `setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on`.

lessons.title: AppArmor and other MAC systems, compared
lessons.goal:
Learn how AppArmor differs from SELinux, and check what this kernel actually has.

Why it matters: Ubuntu and SUSE use AppArmor, Red Hat family systems use SELinux. You will meet both. The ideas (confine programs by policy) are the same; the model and tools differ.

setup.note: Steps with sudo create a test web directory `/srv/lab` and a copy of `cat` labelled as a web server binary, then remove both. Needs SELinux in enforcing mode (the default on Oracle Linux and Red Hat).
commands: sudo rm -rf /srv/lab /usr/local/bin/lab-cat; sudo semanage fcontext -d '/srv/lab(/.*)?' 2>/dev/null; true

steps.title: Which MAC is active here
steps.text: The kernel can load several **Linux Security Modules**. This machine has SELinux. AppArmor is not part of this kernel, so its commands cannot run here.

run.cmd: cat /sys/kernel/security/lsm | tr ',' '\n' | grep -E '^(selinux|apparmor|yama|bpf)$' | tr '\n' ' '; echo
[ -d /sys/kernel/security/apparmor ] && echo 'AppArmor is active' || echo 'AppArmor is not active in this kernel'
run.output: AppArmor is not active in this kernel

steps.title: The model difference
steps.text:
- **SELinux** labels every object (files, processes, ports) with a context stored in the file system, and a policy relates types. It is powerful and uniform, but complex.
- **AppArmor** is **path based**: a profile per program lists the paths it may read, write or execute, and the capabilities and network access it may use. Files have no label. It is simpler to write and read.

Both enforce **mandatory** rules that the confined program (even as root) cannot change.

steps.title: What an AppArmor profile looks like
steps.text: This is a typical profile (it would live in `/etc/apparmor.d/`). It is shown as a file you could save; the commands to load it are marked as explanation only, because AppArmor is not available on this system.

run.cmd: sudo cp usr.sbin.example-daemon /etc/apparmor.d/ && sudo apparmor_parser -r /etc/apparmor.d/usr.sbin.example-daemon
run.reason: AppArmor is not part of this kernel; this is how you would load the profile on Ubuntu

run.cmd: sudo aa-status

steps.after: Reading it: `/etc/example/** r,` the daemon may read everything under /etc/example; `/var/log/example.log w,` write one log file; `capability net_bind_service,` bind low ports; `network inet stream,` TCP over IPv4. Everything not listed is denied. Modes: **enforce** (block) and **complain** (log only), switched with `aa-enforce` and `aa-complain`.

steps.title: Choosing and living with it
steps.text: Do not turn the system's MAC off because it is in the way. Learn its log: `ausearch -m avc` for SELinux, `dmesg | grep apparmor` or `journalctl -k | grep DENIED` for AppArmor. Use the tools that generate rules from observed behaviour (`audit2allow`, `aa-genprof`) only after you understand what is being allowed.

run.cmd: sestatus | grep -E 'Current mode' | tr -s ' ' ' '

steps.under: Both frameworks sit in the same place: the **LSM hooks** in the kernel (`security_file_open`, `security_socket_connect`, ...). They can be stacked in recent kernels. Other LSMs: **Yama** (ptrace scope), **Landlock** (unprivileged self-sandboxing), **BPF LSM** (policy written as eBPF programs), **IMA/EVM** (file integrity) and **lockdown**.

quiz.q: How does AppArmor identify what a profile applies to?
Which distributions use SELinux by default?
options: Red Hat family (RHEL, Oracle Linux, Fedora)

quiz.q: What can a confined root process do to its own MAC policy?
options: Nothing: policy changes need a privileged, unconfined admin domain
quiz.explain: Mandatory means the confined process cannot change it.

quiz.q: Which is the AppArmor equivalent of SELinux permissive mode?

check.scenario: You must confine a new internal daemon on Ubuntu servers and on Oracle Linux servers. What do you do on each?
check.answer: Ubuntu: write an AppArmor profile (`aa-genprof`), run in complain mode while testing, then enforce. Oracle Linux: run the service in its own domain, either with an existing policy or a new module (`sepolicy generate`, `audit2allow`), test in permissive for that domain only (`semanage permissive -a my_t`), then enforce. Also use systemd sandboxing on both for the common baseline.

interview.q: What is SELinux and how does it differ from normal permissions?
interview.a: A mandatory access control system: policy decides which process types may access which object types, regardless of owner or mode, and even root is bound by it. See [the lesson](#/lesson/35/selinux-basics).

interview.q: A service gets Permission denied but the mode is correct. What do you do?
interview.a: Check for an SELinux denial: `ausearch -m avc -ts recent`, compare `ls -Z` with what the policy expects, fix the label with `semanage fcontext` + `restorecon`, or a boolean. See [the workflow](#/lesson/35/selinux-labels-booleans-denials).
chcon sets a label directly and is lost when files are relabelled. restorecon applies the policy's file-context rules (which you extend with semanage fcontext) and is permanent.
Policy switches for common variations, such as httpd_can_network_connect. Query with getsebool, set with setsebool (-P for persistent).

SELinux: label-based, system-wide policy, more expressive and complex. AppArmor: path-based profiles per program, easier to write. Both are LSMs enforcing mandatory rules. See [the comparison](#/lesson/35/apparmor-and-mac).
Briefly, to find out whether SELinux is the cause or to collect all denials of a new application. Prefer per-domain permissive (`semanage permissive -a TYPE`) to system-wide.

glossary.def: Security-Enhanced Linux: label-based mandatory access control in the kernel.
The user:role:type:level label of a process or object.
SELinux policy that allows access by type pairs (domain to object type).
An audit record of an SELinux access vector check that was denied.
A policy switch that enables or disables a behaviour.
Resets file labels to what the policy says they should be.
Path-based mandatory access control used by Ubuntu and SUSE.
